candidates.attacker_control: The value passed by the application into a method parameter annotated with @Path. Retrofit's API is designed for this value to come from runtime data (ids, usernames, file names, search terms). It is converted to a String by the configured `Converter<T, String>` (or Object.toString via BuiltInConverters.ToStringConverter, Converter.java:57-78 / BuiltInConverters.java:89-95) and then inserted directly. Example shapes: `@GET("v1/users/{id}/details")` with `id = ".."`; `@GET("users/{name}")` with `@Path(value="name", encoded=true)` and `name = "../../admin"` (the changelog even records that `/` is intentionally not encoded for encoded=true).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) With the default `encoded = false`, `/` and `%` are percent-encoded (RequestBuilder.java:103), so multi-segment injection requires `encoded = true`; the finding therefore relies mainly on `.`/`..` surviving (verified: `.` is not in the always-encode set at line 33 nor under the 0x20/0x7f range checks). (2) Null path values are rejected (ParameterHandler.java:95-98), and @Path names/templates are validated (ServiceMethod.java:725-734), but no value-side validation exists. (3) Searched the whole tree for "traversal", "URL_PATH_TRAVERSAL" and `".."` — no guard anywhere. (4) OkHttp's HttpUrl dot-segment normalization (which makes the final URL drop the intended prefix) is a dependency behavior not present in the snapshot and was not runtime-verified; even if some layer forwarded a raw `..` path, common server/proxy normalization would still route it differently. (5) The @Path javadoc (http/Path.java:28-51) only promises URL encoding of values, which does not prevent dot-segment traversal and may lead developers to treat raw string values as safe.
candidates.impact: A request issued through the app's Retrofit client can be diverted to a different path on the same configured host than the API interface intended (for example out of a per-tenant/user prefix). Where path prefixes are used for routing or authorization (gateway/microservice routing, servlet path-based access rules), this can bypass those checks, reach unintended internal endpoints, or issue state-changing calls against the wrong resource. Impact is bounded to the configured authority (no cross-host redirect via @Path), and depends on the application passing untrusted data into @Path and on path normalization.
candidates.prerequisites: A service interface in the reviewed application declares a @Path parameter whose value can be influenced by an untrusted party, and the application does not independently sanitize it. With default encoding, traversal needs `..` segments (a single `..` removes one path segment, and multiple @Path parameters can chain). With `encoded = true`, a single value can inject `/` plus `..` segments. End-to-end request rewriting additionally depends on dot-segment normalization by OkHttp's HttpUrl (okhttp 3.10.0 is a declared dependency but its source is not in this snapshot) or by the receiving server/proxy — not verifiable here.
candidates.root_cause: `RequestBuilder.addPathParam` (retrofit/src/main/java/retrofit2/RequestBuilder.java:89-95) performs a raw `relativeUrl.replace("{" + name + "}", canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded))` with no rejection of `.`/`..` segments and no validation that the substituted value stays within its path segment. `canonicalizeForPath` (lines 97-144) percent-encodes only a fixed set (`PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET = " \"<>^`{}|\\?#"`, line 33) plus `/` and `%` when `alreadyEncoded == false` (line 103); the dot character is never encoded, so `..` survives in both modes, and when `encoded = true` `/` and `%` also pass through verbatim, letting one parameter inject whole path segments. The composed relative URL is then handed to OkHttp in `build()` (lines 189-202) via either `urlBuilder.build()` (baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl), line 149) or `baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl)` (line 197), where dot-segments are collapsed, so the intended path prefix can be traversed away. No equivalent guard exists anywhere else in the tree (searches for "traversal", "URL_PATH_TRAVERSAL", and ".." return nothing).
candidates.title: Path traversal via unvalidated @Path parameter value in RequestBuilder.addPathParam
candidates.trace: ServiceMethod.parseParameterAnnotation (ServiceMethod.java:388-405) wires a @Path parameter to `new ParameterHandler.Path<>(name, converter, encoded)`; ParameterHandler.Path.apply (ParameterHandler.java:94-100) calls `builder.addPathParam(name, valueConverter.convert(value), encoded)`; RequestBuilder.addPathParam (line 94) replaces the `{name}` token in the developer-supplied template with the canonicalized attacker value; canonicalizeForPath (lines 97-144) leaves `.` (and, for encoded=true, `/` and `%`) unencoded; RequestBuilder.build (lines 189-202) resolves the modified relative URL against the fixed base URL, and OkHttp's URL resolution collapses `..` segments, so the final request path can be outside the intended endpoint. Note: `relativeUrl` is only mutated by @Path substitution or by @Url (`setRelativeUrl`, lines 73-75), and @Path and @Url are mutually exclusive (ServiceMethod.java:366-374), so this is the only route for parameter-driven path rewriting.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test or exploit was executed. Whether OkHttp 3.10's HttpUrl collapses `..` segments before sending (dependency source absent), whether a given deployed proxy/server normalizes `..`, and whether any specific application passes attacker-controlled data into a @Path parameter are all unverified. The severity is deployment-dependent.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper input validation / path traversal in URL construction (client-side request-path manipulation)

coverage_summary: All 184 assigned files were visible (no binary/sensitive/size exclusions reported). Key core paths were read in full or in relevant part: RequestBuilder, ParameterHandler, ServiceMethod, OkHttpCall, Utils, Converter, BuiltInConverters, ExecutorCallAdapterFactory, DefaultCallAdapterFactory, Platform, Response/Call/Callback; converters (gson, jackson, jaxb, simplexml, moshi, protobuf, scalars, wire, optionals); adapters (rxjava CallArbiter et al., rxjava2, guava, java8, scala); retrofit-mock; samples; pom/build scripts. The P1 relation index covers 182 of 184 files and parsed all 124 Java files with no parse errors, but has no control-flow or data-flow analysis and 1388 unresolved calls; its CALLS/CONTAINS edges for addPathParam -> canonicalizeForPath and ParameterHandler.Path.apply -> addPathParam were used only as navigation and were verified against source text. Not deeply reviewed: website assets, most README/CONTRIBUTING/prose files, and the pom module wiring beyond version/dependency inspection.
limitations: The central `retrofit/src/main/java/retrofit2/Retrofit.java` (and `Retrofit.Builder`, which validates baseUrl and resolves string converters) is absent from the assigned snapshot even though other files reference the class, so the configuration/entry-point code could not be inspected and the snapshot is not self-contained.
No test sources are present in the snapshot, so existing test expectations around @Path/@Url handling could not be checked.

OkHttp/Okio (the actual URL canonicalization and request objects) and the StAX/JAXB runtime are dependencies whose sources are not in the snapshot; their dot-segment/DTD behavior is asserted from API knowledge, not verified here.
No code, tests, builds, or scanners were executed, and no runtime or network behavior was observed; the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The relation index has no semantic resolution or data-flow; taint propagation from application inputs to @Path parameters is demonstrated by API design rather than traced in a concrete app in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Potential XXE in retrofit-converters/jaxb JaxbResponseConverter: `XMLInputFactory.newInstance()` is created with default properties (JaxbResponseConverter.java:29) and used to parse the response body (line 41) without disabling DTDs/external entities, so a malicious or compromised server (or MITM) returning XML could trigger external entity resolution on the client (file read/SSRF).
rejected_leads.reason: Real hardening gap, but attacker control in the normal threat model is the remote endpoint, not an untrusted request parameter, so impact requires a malicious/compromised server or TLS interception; the effective default behavior of the StAX provider on the runtime JDK is external to the snapshot and unverified. Kept as an unconfirmed secondary lead rather than the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SimpleXML converter delegates XML parsing to the third-party org.simpleframework.xml Persister/Serializer (SimpleXmlConverterFactory.java:37-45, SimpleXmlResponseBodyConverter.java:34-48), which may or may not resolve external entities.
rejected_leads.reason: Third-party library source is not in the snapshot; no evidence available either way.

rejected_leads.lead: `@Url` accepts a full URL (ParameterHandler.RelativeUrl, ServiceMethod.java:362-386), so a caller-supplied value can point at any host (SSRF-style).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of @Url (override the base URL); it is only a vulnerability if the application passes untrusted input to it, which is application logic, not a defect in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: `@Query/@Field` with encoded=true and `@Header` values could allow query/header injection.
rejected_leads.reason: encoded=true explicitly means the value is already encoded; OkHttp header value validation is not verifiable from the snapshot, and no concrete injection path was found in the reviewed code.

rejected_leads.lead: OkHttpCall.enqueue catch blocks swallow Throwable/Errors from callbacks with only printStackTrace (OkHttpCall.java:117-126, 133-138), potentially hiding OutOfMemoryError/fatal errors.
rejected_leads.reason: Robustness/error-handling concern with no attacker-controlled input or direct security impact; not a reportable finding here.

summary: Assigned snapshot is a Retrofit (com.squareup.retrofit2) tree at version 2.4.0: 184 files (124 Java) covering the core retrofit module, adapters (guava/java8/rxjava/rxjava2/scala), converters (gson/jackson/jaxb/moshi/protobuf/scalars/simplexml/wire/optionals), retrofit-mock, samples, and build/CI scripts. The strongest source-evidenced issue is in the core request builder: @Path parameter values are substituted into the relative URL with no check against `.`/`..` path segments. `canonicalizeForPath` deliberately leaves `.` untouched (and leaves `/` and `%` untouched when `encoded = true`), so an attacker-influenced path parameter can move the request to a different path on the same host once the relative URL is resolved/canonicalized against the base URL. A weaker, unselected lead is the JAXB converter parsing response XML with an unhardened `XMLInputFactory` (potential client-side XXE). No runtime execution, tests, or external data were used; OkHttp (the URL canonicalizer) and the JAXB/StAX runtime are dependencies not present in the snapshot, so their exact behavior is unverified.
